title: Annotatio I §.II: No Protestant fight on the first two; only the third remains — is the literal sense proper or improper?
pass_a_gloss: But on the prior two significations of taking the words κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, or of retaining them τῷ ῥητῷ, there is no litigation among Protestants, both parties being persuaded that both whatever formal and equipollent Words, and the genuine sense of both sorts of words — that is, always one and the same, the true one agreeing with Christ’s mind — are to be held and kept, so that only the third remains in doubt and controversial. It is confirmed: namely that the controversial literal sense of the words, viewed in the proposition, reduces to this: Whether the Literal Sense is proper, or rather improper?
pass_b_english: On the first two meanings Protestants have no lawsuit: both sides hold the formal (and equipollent) words, and one genuine sense that fits Christ’s mind.
Only the third stays doubtful and contested.
So the disputed “literal” sense of the words in the proposition reduces to this: is that literal sense proper, or improper?
source_text: Enimverò de prioribus duabus significationibus τοῦ capiendi verba κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, vel τῷ ῥητῷ retinendi, litigium nullum inter Protestantes, utrâque parte persuasâ, tam Verba formalia & aequipollentia quaecunque, quàm verborum utrorumque sensum genuinum, h. e. semper unum eundemque, verum illum mentique Christi convenientem, tenendum servandumque esse, ut sola tertia in dubio maneat & controversa. Confirmatur: scil. literalem verborum, in propositione spectatorum, controversum sensum ad hoc recidere: Num Sensus literalis, proprius, an verò improprius sit?

choices.english: to reduce / fall back to this

notes: No fight on 1–2; only proper vs improper remains.
